newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aussie dlr technically unsound as support cracks.
newsitem.headline: Aussie dlr technically unsound as support cracks.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished with widespread losses Wednesday, but did recover from early lows in a seesaw session characterised by heavy two-way flows.

The currency was battered by agrressive selling from a U.S. investment bank which was joined by Swiss and Japanese offers to see it trough at US$0.7735. Dealers said good bids emerged there to help recover US$0.7760, but reckoned it was technically unsound while beneath 78 cents and vulnerable to further falls.
There was a moment of relief when the Reserve Bank resisted the temptation to ease following Tuesday's board meeting, but crucial developments Thursday meant it was too soon to relax.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was hovering at US$0.7756/61 after dipping as far as US$0.7736/41 from an early US$0.7764/69 and US$0.7794/99 late here Tuesday.
Support was now pegged at US$0.7735 and US$0.7720, while resistance was lined up at US$0.7770 and US$0.7790.
Traders said a locally-based U.S. investment bank had led the rout overnight and was in the driving seat this morning, forcing the break of US$0.7760 and triggering stop loss sales.
A number of respected U.S. funds were also seen lightening positions amid talk of a strategic switch to sterling assets following a rise in U.K. interest rates Tuesday.
Japanese equity houses were also serious sellers of AUD/yen reversing recent demand related to yen/A$ samurai issues.
Traders said the yen was showing a sudden sensitivity to Japanese asset prices in the belief a sustained rise in share and bond yields might presage a tightening in official policy.
Most analysts thought the speculation premature, but it was enough to knock the dollar to 97.38/48 yen from 98.07/17 late Tuesday and 99.04/14 the day before.
Ground was also lost to sterling which not only enjoyed a rate hike but received a big boost to offshore confidence when the new Labour government made the Bank of England independent.
The hike left U.K. rates 0.25 point above official rates here and the market was discounting more, so giving the pound a healthy interest differential over the A$ on shorter-dated debt.
This drew recommendations from some banks, including SBC, to sell Aussie and buy sterling and there were signs funds had heard with the A$ down at 0.4740/46 stg from 0.4808/15 Tuesday.
The weakness on the crosses contributed to a 0.4 point loss on the dollar's trade weighted index to 60.3.
The local currency could not entirely shake speculation domestic interest rates were heading lower, despite the silence of the RBA at its first window of opportunity this morning.
The RBA's inactivity would usually have been taken as a sign a cut was off the agenda this month, but in this case there was a risk jobs data Thursday could yet all calculations.
It was surprise falls in employment for February and March which had first stirred talk of another easing and a further fall in April would put the RBA under intense pressure to cut.
Most analysts, however, expect employment to bounce back by around 35,000 after a 33,900 fall the month before.
A clearer guide to current RBA thinking should emerge tomorrow when governor Ian Macfarlane gives his first testimony on the course of monetary policy to a Parliamentary committee.

The bank's position on policy and its latest assessment of the economy will be released at 10.00 am (0000 GMT), while Macfarlane is expected to start speaking from 10.15 onwards and will be answering questions from the committee afterwards.
The testimony could well last beyond the release of the jobs data at 11.30 am, so he may also face questions on the result.

Elsewhere, the government announced the sale of three Federal airports for A$3.3 billion, confirming long running market rumours. Traders said there were few forex implications but it would help put the budget in surplus for 1996/97.
